draft.title: Test crosses
card: An individual with a dominant phenotype could be homozygous dominant (AA) or heterozygous (Aa). Both look the same, so the genotype cannot be told by looking.
A test cross mates this individual with a homozygous recessive (aa). The aa partner can only pass on a, so it does not hide any allele in the offspring.
If the individual is AA, all offspring get one A and show the dominant trait.
If the individual is Aa, about half the offspring are Aa (dominant) and half are aa (recessive). Even one recessive offspring shows the individual is heterozygous.
draft.remember: A recessive offspring from a test cross means the tested parent carries a recessive allele.

a.q: Why is a homozygous recessive individual used as the partner in a test cross?
opts: It can only pass on a recessive allele
It always passes on a dominant allele
It makes the recessive trait disappear
a.why: The partner gives only a recessive allele, so the tested parent's alleles show in the offspring phenotypes. Making all offspring heterozygous only happens if the tested parent is AA, so it is not the reason for the choice.
a.clue: What can the aa partner pass on?

b.q: Kofi has a black-coated guinea pig. Black (B) is dominant over brown (b). He crosses it with a brown guinea pig and gets six black and two brown young. What is the genotype of the black parent?
opts: BB, as most young are black
Not possible to tell from this cross
b.why: A brown young must be bb, so it got a b from each parent. The black parent therefore carries b and is Bb. Having mostly black young does not mean BB, as a Bb parent gives about half black.
b.clue: Where did the brown young get a b allele from?

a.best: It can only pass on a recessive allele
